summary: Satellite Evolution is an interactive web app that turns NASA satellite data into clear answers about how Earth is changing. It has two parts. First, a timeline film: users drag a year slider through 63 years of NASA missions, from Explorer 1 (1958) to the James Webb Space Telescope (2021), while each satellite mechanically transforms into the next. Each stop shows a card with mission facts and a link to the NASA source. Second, the Trend Detective. It selects four NASA satellite records: global surface temperature (GISTEMP), Arctic sea ice, the Antarctic ozone hole and global sea level. For each one it answers the challenge's questions: what changes, where (by latitude band), how much (total change and rate per year) and whether the trend is statistically significant (Sen's slope and the Mann-Kendall test). The results: Earth warmed 0.93 °C since 1980, with the Arctic warming about 3 times faster; September sea ice fell 45%; sea level rose 97 mm and is accelerating; ozone recovery is visible but not yet significant. This matters because it makes real NASA data understandable for anyone, in English or Russian, on any device.
details:
Satellite Evolution is a web app that connects NASA's satellites with what they discovered about Earth.

What it does

1. Timeline film: drag a year slider (or scroll, swipe, use arrow keys) through 63 years of NASA missions, from Explorer 1 (1958) to the James Webb Space Telescope (2021). The video stops at each of 18 satellites, and each one mechanically transforms into the next. A card shows launch date, vehicle, mass, orbit, mission goal and key result, with a link to the NASA mission page.

2. Trend Detective: selects four NASA Earth records — global surface temperature (GISTEMP v4), Arctic September sea ice, the Antarctic ozone hole and global sea level — and answers the challenge questions: what changes, where (8 latitude bands), how much (total change and rate per year) and whether it is significant (Sen's slope + Mann–Kendall test, α = 0.05). It opens from the satellite that measured the data (Terra, Aqua, Aura, Sentinel-6), and a marker shows the year you are viewing.

Results: +0.93 °C since 1980 with the Arctic warming ~3× faster; −45% September sea ice; +97 mm sea level since 1993 and accelerating; ozone recovery visible but not yet significant. We show the "not yet" honestly instead of overstating it.

Benefits and impact: people first get curious about the satellites, then see real, tested evidence of change. It works on phones, in English and Russian, with no installation.

Tools: JavaScript (Vite), HTML/CSS, SVG charts, Web Audio, Node.js scripts for statistics, ffmpeg for video, GitHub Pages hosting. All trend numbers are computed by an open script from the original data files included in the repository.

Creativity: the film turns the history of NASA technology into one continuous story, and the data panel links each trend back to the spacecraft that measured it.

What we considered: scientific honesty (robust statistics, significance shown openly), accessibility (keyboard, mobile layout, two languages), a small download (under 35 MB) and clear labelling of AI-generated visuals.
